summaries.example: Imagine a number path that starts 1, 2, 3, and keeps going. No matter how far you travel, you can always name a larger number. This shows one idea of infinity: having no final number. But infinity can be puzzling. A hotel with infinitely many rooms could be full and still make room for another guest by moving each guest to the next room.
summaries.summary: Infinity is the idea of having no final limit. The entry explains that this idea has several meanings. In ordinary speech, “infinite” can mean enormous. In philosophy, it can mean boundless or endless. In mathematics, it can describe numbers, lengths, collections, and processes. Ancient thinkers such as Aristotle distinguished potential infinity from actual infinity: a line may be divided again and again, but that does not mean all the divisions exist together as a completed collection. Over time, mathematicians found ways to study infinity more exactly. They used limits to describe quantities that get closer and closer to a value, and they developed methods for comparing infinite collections. Cantor showed that there are different sizes of infinity, not just one. The entry also explains why infinity can lead to surprising puzzles. A full infinite hotel may accept new guests, and an infinite process may raise questions about what happens at its end. Similar issues appear in probability, decision-making, and ideas about the size and shape of space. Infinity is therefore both a powerful mathematical tool and a source of philosophical questions.
key_ideas: Infinity can mean different things: something endless, a mathematical collection, or a process that can continue without stopping.
People in history disagreed about whether completed infinite things are possible. Aristotle accepted processes that could continue forever but rejected completed infinite sizes.
Mathematicians developed careful methods for working with infinity, including limits, infinite sums, and ways to compare infinite collections.
Some infinite collections behave surprisingly. The natural numbers can be paired with their square numbers, even though the squares are only some of the natural numbers.
Infinity helps mathematics, but it also creates puzzles about counting, motion, probability, choices, and space.
summaries.why_it_matters: Infinity appears whenever we think about endless counting, repeated division, very large collections, or space and time. Learning about it helps us understand why ordinary ideas about size and counting do not always work for infinite things. It also shows how philosophy and mathematics work together: puzzles can reveal hidden assumptions, while mathematical definitions can make vague ideas more precise.

important_terms.definition: Something with no end, boundary, or limit. In mathematics, it can describe a process or collection that is not finite.
A process that can continue forever, even though each step is still finite.
A completed infinite collection or quantity, treated as existing all at once in a mathematical theory.
A rule for finding the size of a collection by pairing every item in one collection with exactly one item in another.
A number system used for counting, beginning 1, 2, 3, and so on.
A process with infinitely many steps that are finished in a limited amount of time.

questions_to_think_about: Is doing something forever the same as finishing infinitely many steps?
Can a collection have the same size as one of its proper parts?
Why might an infinite hotel be full and still have room?
Are mathematical infinities found in the world, or are they tools made by mathematicians?

summaries.example: Consider the natural numbers and the square numbers: 1, 2, 3, 4, ... and 1, 4, 9, 16, ... . The square numbers form a proper subset of the natural numbers, so a part-whole intuition suggests that there should be fewer squares. Yet the function n ↦ n² pairs each natural number with exactly one square, and every square appears. Cantorian cardinality therefore assigns these two sets the same size. The example shows why finite intuitions about size cannot simply be transferred to infinite collections.
summaries.summary: The entry surveys infinity as a concept in philosophy and mathematics, with particular attention to mathematical developments and their philosophical consequences. It distinguishes loose uses of “infinite” from strict qualitative and mathematical uses. Historically, Greek thinkers confronted infinite divisibility, endless number sequences, and Zeno-style paradoxes while often avoiding completed infinities in public mathematical arguments. Aristotle’s influential distinction between potential and actual infinity allowed indefinitely repeatable operations but rejected completed infinite magnitudes in his physical framework. Early modern mathematics increasingly employed infinitary methods: Cavalieri’s indivisibles, Desargues’s points at infinity, and the infinitesimals of the calculus. Nineteenth-century analysis replaced informal infinitesimals with limit definitions, although non-standard analysis later supplied rigorous systems containing infinitesimal and infinitely large numbers. Cantor transformed the study of infinite collections. A bijection defines equal cardinality, even when one set is a proper subset of another; ordinals instead track positions in well-orderings. Countable and uncountable sets form different levels, and the power-set operation produces a strictly larger cardinality. These theories raise ontological questions about whether infinite mathematical objects exist, while finitism, intuitionism, and predicativism limit or revise commitments to them. The later discussion applies infinity to paradoxes, probability, decision theory, and space-time. Infinite hotels, supertasks, divergent expectations, infinite utility, and cosmological models show that familiar finite principles may fail or require qualification. key_ideas: The entry separates qualitative ideas of boundlessness from mathematical ideas involving quantities, measures, processes, and collections.
Aristotle’s potential/actual distinction shaped later debates. His view allowed indefinite division and succession while rejecting completed infinite magnitudes in his physical picture.

Greek mathematics often presented results without explicit actual infinities, using exhaustion; early modern geometry and calculus then used indivisibles, points at infinity, and infinitesimals more openly.
Limits and infinite sums give rigorous ways to represent processes approaching values. Extended real numbers are useful in some contexts but do not support unrestricted arithmetic such as +∞ + −∞.
Cantor’s theory distinguishes ordinals, which describe order type, from cardinals, which describe size. It yields countable and uncountable infinities and an unending hierarchy of cardinalities.
Infinity generates philosophical problems in ontology, probability, decision theory, and cosmology. The source presents competing responses rather than one final solution to every puzzle.
summaries.why_it_matters: Infinity is not merely a very large number. It changes the rules governing comparison, addition, limits, probability, and decision. Studying it clarifies why mathematical definitions matter and why different structures—real numbers, cardinals, ordinals, or hyperreals—answer different questions. It also connects abstract mathematics with debates about what kinds of objects, processes, or spaces could exist.

important_terms.definition: A quantity or collection without a finite bound. The word also has non-mathematical uses, such as “boundless” or “immense.”
Infinity understood as an indefinitely repeatable process, where every completed stage remains finite.
Infinity understood as a completed totality or object, such as an infinite set treated as a whole.
A mathematical assignment of a distinct number to each position in a well-ordered collection.
A number answering a “how many?” question; for infinite sets, it is determined by whether a bijection exists.
A pairing between two sets in which each member of either set is paired with exactly one member of the other.
A number smaller in absolute value than every positive finite real number but not equal to zero, in a suitable non-Archimedean system.
A space that has no boundary but may still have finite total extent, as in a model based on a 3-sphere.

questions_to_think_about: Does the success of a mathematical theory show that its infinite objects exist, or only that the theory is useful and consistent within its framework?
Should size for infinite sets be governed by bijection, by the part-whole principle, or by different notions for different purposes?
Why can a finite line be unbounded in some geometries, and why does this challenge the identification of infinity with unboundedness?
Do supertasks show that an infinite sequence of actions can be completed, or do they expose missing physical details?
What should a decision theory say when expected utility is infinite or when an infinite series fails to converge?

summaries.example: Suppose a library has rooms numbered 1, 2, 3, and so on, with every room occupied. A new reader arrives. The librarian can move the reader in room 1 to room 2, the reader in room 2 to room 3, and so on. Room 1 is now free. For a finite library this would be impossible, but for an infinite collection it follows from pairing the old rooms with the new room numbers.
summaries.summary: Infinity is an old philosophical question and a central mathematical idea. The entry begins by separating several meanings of the term. Something may be called infinite because it is huge, because it has no boundary, or because it is represented by a mathematical process or collection with no finite limit. Ancient philosophers studied these ideas through questions about the universe, motion, time, and division. Aristotle made a major distinction between potential infinity and actual infinity. A segment can be divided again and again, but, on his view, that does not mean it consists of infinitely many completed pieces. Greek mathematicians often avoided mentioning actual infinity in their final proofs by using the method of exhaustion. In the seventeenth century, mathematicians used indivisibles, points at infinity, and infinitesimals to develop new geometric and calculus techniques. Later work made these methods more rigorous through limits, while non-standard analysis created rigorous systems with infinitesimals. Cantor’s theory changed how infinite collections are compared. A bijection can show that two collections have the same cardinality, even when one is a proper subset of the other. It also reveals that there are different sizes of infinity, including countable and uncountable collections. The entry then considers philosophical questions about the existence of mathematical infinities and puzzles involving infinite hotels, supertasks, probability, decision-making, and space-time. It does not treat every dispute as settled; instead, it shows how different assumptions lead to different conclusions.
key_ideas: The word “infinite” can mean extremely large, endless, boundless, or mathematically non-finite; these meanings should not be mixed together.
Aristotle accepted potential infinity but questioned actual infinity. This distinction influenced debates about whether infinite collections or magnitudes can really exist.
Mathematical history moved from avoiding explicit infinity, through exhaustion, to using indivisibles and infinitesimals in geometry and calculus.
Limits describe values approached by a sequence, while infinite sums are defined through limits of their finite partial sums. Some sums converge, and others do not.
Cantor’s approach says that two infinite collections have the same cardinality when a bijection pairs them, even if one is a proper subset of the other.
Infinity creates puzzles in hotel stories, lamps, probability, choices, and theories about whether space is finite or infinite.
summaries.why_it_matters: Infinity helps explain important ideas in calculus, geometry, set theory, probability, and cosmology. It also teaches a broader lesson about reasoning: a rule that works for finite objects may fail for infinite ones. By comparing historical views and modern mathematical frameworks, we can see how definitions, examples, and hidden assumptions shape philosophical arguments.

important_terms.definition: Having no last point, number, or boundary; in mathematics, a way of describing endless processes or non-finite collections.
An endless continuation in which each stage is finite, even though there is no final stage.
A completed infinite collection considered as one whole.
A collection containing every member of another collection, and at least one additional member.
A matching in which every item in one collection is paired with exactly one item in another collection.
The mathematical size of a collection, determined by whether it can be put into a bijection with another collection.
A process with endlessly many stages completed within a finite time.
A number that is smaller than every positive ordinary number but is not zero, in certain extended number systems.

questions_to_think_about: Why does a proper subset usually seem smaller, and why can that rule fail for infinite collections?
Is a process that never ends different from a completed infinite collection?
Why is 0.999... equal to 1 when the dots represent a limit?
Can an infinite sequence of actions happen in a finite time? What extra physical details would matter?
Should mathematical infinity be treated as something real, a useful model, or both?
